findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"}, {"path":
findings.body: owner_id is interpolated directly into the SQL string, so any attacker-controlled value can break out of the quoted literal and execute arbitrary SQL against the orders table. Use a parameter placeholder instead of string formatting.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes owner_id like "x' OR '1'='1" (or a stacked/statement-crafting payload); the query returns rows for other customers or modifies data, causing a full data breach of the billing pipeline.
findings.suggestion: query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
findings.title: Prevent SQL injection by using parameterized queries

findings.body: range(1, len(entries)) skips entries[0], so the first entry is silently dropped from the ranked output. The iteration should cover every element; use range(len(entries)) or iterate directly.

findings.title: Start the loop at 1 to skip the first entry

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default [] is created once at function definition and shared across all calls. events.append(event_type) mutates it, so events accumulate across unrelated calls and the returned mapping contains events from previous invocations.
findings.failure_scenario: Two sequential calls register_shipment_events("a") then register_shipment_events("b"); the second call's result contains ["a", "b"] instead of ["b"].

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest identifier "in constant time", but the implementation sorts the entire records list, which is O(n log n). A docstring that contradicts the code misleads callers making performance assumptions.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relies on the documented constant-time guarantee and uses newest_queue_id in a hot loop, causing unexpected O(n log n) work per call on large record sets.
findings.suggestion:
"""Return the newest queue identifier by creation timestamp.

    Sorts the records, so this runs in O(n log n) time.
    """
findings.title: Fix the newest_queue_id docstring: it is not constant time

findings.body: unique_payment_labels checks membership with `if label in seen` where seen is a list, making the deduplication loop O(n²) as each lookup scans the list linearly. The cost scales quadratically with the number of payment rows.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large list of payment rows (e.g. tens of thousands), each new label triggers a linear scan of all previously seen labels, causing noticeably slow deduplication that scales quadratically with input size.
findings.suggestion: if label in seen_set:
findings.title: Use a set for seen labels to avoid O(n²) scans

findings.body: newest_queue_id sorts all records (O(n log n) plus a full copy) only to read the last element. A single max() pass finds the newest record in O(n) without building a sorted copy.
findings.failure_scenario: For large record lists, an unnecessary O(n log n) sort and full list copy is performed on every call, adding avoidable CPU and allocation cost in a helper that may be called frequently.
findings.title: Sort the whole list just to find the newest record

findings.body: The inner double loop over zones and weights computes the same count for every carrier, since the count does not depend on the carrier. The nested scan is re-executed len(carriers) times, multiplying work by the number of carriers for no benefit.
findings.failure_scenario: With many carriers and large zone/weight lists, the identical O(zones*weights) computation is repeated once per carrier, inflating runtime linearly with carrier count for a result that could be computed once.
findings.title: Hoist the carrier-independent zone/weight count out of the loop

findings.body: load_order_rows executes a SELECT with no LIMIT and materialises every matching row via fetchall(), so memory usage and latency scale with the full size of the owner's orders table rather than the rows actually needed by callers.
findings.failure_scenario: For an owner with a very large number of orders, the call fetches and builds a dict for every row at once, spiking memory and blocking the caller on a single large result set.
findings.title: Unbounded query loads the entire orders result set into memory

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"'}, {
findings.body: The new load_order_rows builds a SQL query by interpolating owner_id directly into the statement. Any caller-controlled value can break out of the string literal and execute arbitrary SQL against the orders table (read, modify, or exfiltrate data). Use a parameterized query instead.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies owner_id like "x' OR '1'='1" (or a UNION/DELETE payload); the query executes attacker-chosen SQL, exposing or corrupting all customer order data.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation of owner_id

findings.body: range(1, len(entries)) skips entries[0], so the first invoice entry is never scored or returned. With a single-entry list the function returns an empty list.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller ranks a list of invoice entries; the highest-priority first entry is silently dropped from the output, and a one-entry input yields [].
findings.suggestion: for position in range(0, len(entries))):
findings.title: Start the ranking loop at index 0 to include the first entry

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: register_shipment_events uses events: list[str] = [] as a default. The default list is created once at function definition and shared across all calls, so events accumulate across unrelated invocations and the returned mapping contains events from previous calls.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events("ship") twice returns {"ship": ["ship", "ship"]} on the second call instead of {"ship": ["ship"]}, corrupting event records.
findings.title: Remove the mutable default argument

findings.body: flag_large_backorder_totals accepts a threshold parameter but the comparison hardcodes 5000, so callers cannot change the review threshold and the parameter is silently ignored.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passing threshold=1000 still gets only rows above 5000, so backorders between 1000 and 5000 that should be flagged for review are silently missed.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: The docstring promises the newest queue identifier 'in constant time', but the implementation sorts all records by created_at, which is O(n log n). The documented complexity is false and will mislead maintainers reasoning about performance.
findings.failure_scenario: A maintainer relies on the documented constant-time guarantee and calls newest_queue_id in a hot loop; the hidden sort degrades performance as the record list grows.
findings.suggestion: """Return the newest queue identifier by created_at, or None if empty."""
findings.title: Correct the newest_queue_id docstring's constant-time claim

findings.anchor: def flag_large_backorder_totals(rows: list[dict[str, object]], threshold: float) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: The docstring says rows are flagged when their total crosses the review threshold, but the function ignores its threshold parameter entirely and compares against a hardcoded 5000. The documented contract contradicts the implementation, so callers passing a threshold will get unexpected results and the docstring misleads them.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=100) expecting rows over 100 to be flagged; rows between 100 and 5000 are silently omitted.
findings.suggestion: """Flag backorder rows whose total exceeds 5000."""
findings.title: Fix the flag_large_backorder_totals docstring to match its behavior

findings.anchor: Assumes records arrive in chronological order.
findings.body: The docstring states 'Assumes records arrive in chronological order', yet the implementation sorts by created_at and does not rely on arrival order. This stale assumption confuses readers about the actual contract; either drop the sentence or, if the sort is meant to be removed in favor of trusting order, say so explicitly.
findings.suggestion: """Return the id of the record with the latest created_at value."""
findings.title: Document the chronological-order assumption of newest_queue_id

findings.body: The count is identical for every zone/weight pair — it just multiplies the number of truthy zones by the number of positive weights, so the nested loops and the carrier dimension add nothing a single expression wouldn't. If real per-zone/per-weight viability rules are meant to apply, they're missing; if not, the whole helper collapses to len(zones) * positive-weights per carrier and probably doesn't need to exist.
findings.title: cross_check_tariff_routes ignores zone and weight semantics

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The newly added load_order_rows builds the query with an f-string, embedding owner_id unquoted into the SQL text. Any caller-controlled owner_id containing a quote can terminate the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL, reading or modifying data across owners. This is also unrelated to the stated intent of refactoring pipeline modules.
findings.failure_scenario: A request with owner_id = "x' OR '1'='1" (or worse, a UNION/DELETE payload) makes the query match or mutate rows belonging to other customers, leaking or corrupting order data.
findings.suggestion: cursor.execute("SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", (owner_id,))
findings.title: New SQL query interpolates owner_id directly — SQL injection

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: register_shipment_events uses events: list[str] = [] as a default. The same list object is reused across every call that omits the argument, so events accumulate across calls and the returned mapping contains events from previous invocations. This new function also appears unrelated to the stated refactor intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events("created") twice returns {"created": ["created", "created"]} on the second call instead of ["created"], corrupting event records.
findings.title: Mutable default argument leaks state between calls

findings.body: flag_large_backorder_totals accepts a threshold argument but compares against the literal 5000, so callers cannot change the review cutoff and the parameter is silently ignored. float(row["total"]) also raises KeyError if a row lacks the key, unlike the .get pattern used elsewhere in this codebase.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes threshold=10000 expecting only very large backorders flagged, but rows with totals between 5000 and 10000 are still flagged, producing wrong review queues; a row without 'total' crashes the function.
findings.suggestion: if float(row.get("total", 0)) > threshold:
findings.title: Honor the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000

findings.body: rank_invoice_entries iterates range(1, len(entries)), which silently drops the first entry from the scored list, so the highest-scored element can be missing from the returned ranking.
findings.failure_scenario: With entries = [{score: 99}, {score: 5}], the function returns only the score-5 entry; the top-ranked invoice is omitted from the output.
findings.suggestion: for position in range(len(entries)):
findings.title: Start the ranking loop at index 0, not 1

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. If this stamp is later compared with timezone-aware timestamps (or serialized with an offset expectation), comparisons raise TypeError or record the wrong instant.
findings.failure_scenario: A checkpoint stamped with naive UTC time is compared against an aware datetime elsewhere, raising TypeError, or is interpreted as local time by a consumer, shifting the recorded creation time.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Replace deprecated utcnow with timezone-aware UTC

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"  # then cursor.execute(query)
findings.body: The query is built by string-formatting owner_id directly into the SQL text, so any value containing a quote escapes the literal and injects arbitrary SQL. Use a parameterized query instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes owner_id = "x' OR '1'='1" (or a crafted DROP/UNION payload); the executed statement matches or modifies rows for all customers instead of one owner, leaking or corrupting order data.
findings.suggestion: cursor.execute("SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", (owner_id,))
findings.title: Interpolate owner_id into SQL via f-string

findings.body: The docstring claims constant time, but the implementation sorts all records (O(n log n)) and even contradicts its own 'assumes chronological order' note by re-sorting. Either return records[-1] directly under the stated assumption, or fix the docstring.
findings.title: newest_queue_id is not constant time as documented

findings.anchor: def flag_large_backorder_totals(rows: list[dict[str, object]], threshold: float) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: flag_large_backorder_totals accepts a threshold parameter and its docstring says it flags rows whose total crosses "the review threshold", but the body compares against a hardcoded 5000 and never uses threshold. Either the docstring/signature misleads callers or the parameter is dead; the public surface contradicts its documented contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes threshold=1000 expecting rows above 1000 to be flagged; rows between 1000 and 5000 are silently omitted, so backorders requiring review are missed.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: Document or honor the ignored threshold parameter

findings.anchor: def newest_queue_id(records: list[dict[str, object]]) -> str | None:
findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest queue identifier "in constant time" and that records "arrive in chronological order", but the implementation sorts the full list (O(n log n)) and does not rely on input order at all. The documentation contradicts the code on both points and will mislead callers making performance decisions.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller reading the docstring assumes O(1) behaviour and calls this in a hot loop over large record lists; actual O(n log n) sorting causes measurable latency, and the 'assumes chronological order' note suggests an ordering contract that does not exist.
findings.suggestion: """Return the newest queue identifier by creation timestamp."""
findings.title: Fix the newest_queue_id docstring: it is not constant time

findings.body: The inner double loop over zones and weights does not reference `carrier` at all, so every carrier gets an identical count while paying an O(len(zones) * len(weights) * len(carriers)) triple-nested loop. Compute the viable combination count once and assign it to each carrier.
findings.failure_scenario: With 100 zones, 100 weights and 50 carriers the function performs 500,000 iterations to produce 50 copies of the same number.
findings.title: cross_check_tariff_routes recounts the same total for every carrier

findings.body: The new function computes the same count for every carrier — the zone/weight loops never reference the carrier — so the per-carrier result is identical for all carriers and the 'viable routing combinations per carrier' contract is not met. This new function is also unrelated to the stated refactor intent.
findings.failure_scenario: With carriers ["a", "b"], zones ["z1"], weights [1, 2], the result is {"a": 2, "b": 2} regardless of any carrier-specific viability, misleading routing decisions.
findings.title: cross_check_tariff_routes counts combinations independent of carrier

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"'}, {
findings.body: owner_id is interpolated directly into the SQL text, so any value containing a single quote terminates the string literal and the rest of the value is parsed as SQL. Whoever controls owner_id can rewrite the WHERE clause (e.g. ' OR '1'='1) or append a UNION branch, reading order rows belonging to customers other than the intended owner. Pass the value as a query parameter so the driver escapes it; if this cursor follows the qmark style (e.g. sqlite3), use ? instead of %s.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes owner_id = "' OR '1'='1" (or appends a UNION SELECT); the f-string embeds it verbatim, the WHERE clause matches every row, and the function returns all customers' orders instead of one owner's rows.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Build the order query with a bound parameter, not an f-string

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default events=[] list is created once at function definition and shared across every call that omits it, so events accumulate across calls and the returned dict reflects prior invocations. This is also an out-of-scope new function under a 'refactor' commit message.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events('a') then register_shipment_events('b') returns {'b': ['a', 'b']} instead of {'b': ['b']}.
findings.title: Remove the mutable default argument in register_shipment_events

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. Mixing this naive stamp with aware timestamps elsewhere produces incorrect comparisons and ordering of checkpoints.
findings.failure_scenario: A checkpoint stamped with utcnow() is compared against an aware UTC timestamp; the naive value is interpreted in local time, shifting the checkpoint by the UTC offset and mis-ordering manifests.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware now() instead of deprecated utcnow()

findings.body: unique_payment_labels keeps seen labels in a list and tests membership with `in`, making the deduplication O(n²) in the number of rows. A set gives O(1) membership tests and linear overall behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: With a large payment row list, each label lookup scans the accumulated seen list, so total work grows quadratically and the function becomes a hotspot on big inputs.
findings.suggestion: if label in seen_set:
findings.title: Use a set for the seen-labels check

findings.anchor: def cross_check_tariff_routes(zones: list[str], weights: list[int], carriers: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
findings.body: The docstring says it counts "viable tariff routing combinations per carrier", but the implementation counts every non-empty zone paired with every positive weight identically for every carrier — carrier identity does not affect the count, and no viability check beyond `weight > 0 and zone` is applied. The name and docstring promise more than the code delivers.
findings.suggestion:
"""Count valid zone/weight combinations per carrier.

    Every carrier receives the same count: the number of (zone, weight)
    pairs where the zone is non-empty and the weight is positive.
    """
findings.title: Clarify the cross_check_tariff_routes docstring

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest queue identifier "in constant time", but the implementation sorts the entire records list (O(n log n)) before taking the last element. A docstring that contradicts the code misleads callers making performance decisions.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relies on the documented constant-time guarantee and passes large record lists in a hot path, causing unexpected O(n log n) sorting cost on every call.
findings.suggestion:
"""Return the newest queue identifier by creation timestamp.

    Sorts the records by created_at and returns the last id.
    """
findings.title: Fix the newest_queue_id docstring: it is not constant time

findings.body: newest_queue_id sorts all records (O(n log n)) and builds a full ordered copy just to read the last element; max() with the same key finds the newest record in O(n) without the intermediate list. The docstring's 'constant time' claim is also inaccurate.
findings.failure_scenario: On large record lists the full sort allocates an O(n) copy and does O(n log n) comparisons where a single linear pass suffices.
findings.title: Avoid sorting the whole list to find the newest record

findings.body: cross_check_tariff_routes runs the nested zone/weight loop for every carrier, but the count does not depend on the carrier at all — it is recomputed identically len(carriers) times. Hoist the count out of the carrier loop (or compute it directly from the list lengths) to turn O(c·z·w) into O(z·w) or O(1).
findings.failure_scenario: With many carriers and large zone/weight lists, the same nested scan is repeated per carrier, multiplying work by the carrier count for an identical result.
findings.title: Recompute the zone/weight count once instead of per carrier

findings.body: The commit message claims a refactor, but the diff changes runtime behavior across every module: validation minimums are loosened (e.g. quantity minimums dropped to 1 in cap_refund, reconcile_carrier, balance_payment, annotate_tariff, settle_batch, reconcile_route), notes-length limits and truncation caps are silently altered, and rate-table constants (bracket sizes, residual rates 0.25/0.4/0.5, residual thresholds 0.01/0.05/0.1) are changed with no rationale. These are semantic changes to billing/validation logic, not refactoring, and none are explained by the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously passed validation with quantity 5 now passes with quantity 1 (or 0-adjacent values), and billed amounts change because bracket caps and residual rates differ; downstream consumers see silently different results after a 'refactor' release.
findings.title: Diff contradicts stated intent: behavior changes, not refactoring

findings.body: The same PR that renames parameters also silently changes behavioral constants (quantity minimums, slice caps like ranked[:6]→ranked[:3], bracket sizes, fallback rates). Bundled with pure-rename churn, these one-character business-rule changes are nearly impossible to review or bisect. If the numbers are intentional, split them into their own commit with a rationale; if they are accidental fallout of a generation/rename script, revert them.
findings.failure_scenario: A reviewer skims the diff as a rename pass and approves it; the silent change of e.g. the head_quantity threshold from 63 to 26 or the fallback rate 0.5→0.4 ships to production unreviewed, altering billing and summary outputs.
findings.title: Magic-number threshold edits are indistinguishable from the rename churn
